title: Hera's Didymos asteroid in eclipse

content:
23 NOV. 2026 publication date 706 Views

A solar eclipse in deep space, shown in this early view of the Didymos binary asteroids from the European Space Agency’s Hera mission for planetary defence. The smaller Dimorphos moonlet is seen casting its shadow across part of its Didymos parent body, to blank out the Sun across the shaded stretch of rocky surface.

“Eclipses just like last summer’s total solar eclipse occur on asteroids as well, when they have a small moon like this one,” explains Patrick Michel, Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. “Didymos and Dimorphos are subject to the same celestial mechanics as Earth and the Moon, but at a much smaller scale and lower gravity environment.

Hera logo

“So in principle someone could be sitting on Didymos and have the same kind of eclipse experience – although in practice sitting there would be very difficult because its gravity is so low and it is spinning very fast!”

The scale of Dimorphos’s shadow onto Didymos is due to its proximity: the smaller moon orbits about a kilometre away from Didymos.

Hera approaches Dimorphos

This low velocity is due to the low masses and gravities involved: the Dimorphos moonlet is just 151 m across, about the same size as the Great Pyramid of Giza, while the 730-m diameter Didymos is a bit smaller than Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper. As a result Dimorphos has gravity about 40 000 times weaker than Earth's, while Dimorphos has about 200 000 times weaker gravity than Earth’s.

This image was acquired by Hera’s monochrome Asteroid Framing Camera, employed both for navigation and science imaging.

Hera shown surveying the Dimorphos asteroid.

Hera’s first images to be unveiled

In 2022 the small moonlet of Didymos called Dimorphos was impacted by NASA’s DART spacecraft to shift its orbit around the larger body. Now the European Space Agency’s Hera mission has arrived to perform a close-up ‘crash scene investigation’ of the binary asteroid system, to gather vital data to turn this grand-scale experiment into a well understood and potentially repeatable planetary defence technique.

Join the Hera team on the evening of Wednesday 25 November as they share the first close-up images of this historic transformed space object.

Hera spacecraft during ground testing

Our Hera livestream starts from 19:45 CET on Wednesday 25 November. Follow the livestream on ESA WebTV or the ESA YouTube channel.
